front.title: Delegation Chains in Agent Protocols: Binding Authority and Action into Verifiable Evidence

abstract.t: Agent protocols — A2A-style agent-to-agent calls and MCP-style agent-to-tool calls — increasingly route work through delegation: one agent authorizes another to act, and the delegate acts. When the action is later disputed, the question "whose authority was this under, and what exactly was done" must be answerable from artifacts, not from logs held by the parties to the dispute. This document scopes the problem of delegation evidence: how a delegating agent's grant of authority and a delegate's subsequent actions are bound into verifiable receipts, and how a verifier checks a chain of delegation without trusting any central party. It defines the required evidence at each hop — a signed grant, a signed action record referencing the grant, and receipts witnessed independently of both parties — and states what verification does and does not establish. This document specifies nothing and proposes no wire format; it scopes requirements and identifies the existing machinery that carries them.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The emerging agent protocols share a shape. In agent-to-agent protocols (A2A ), an agent publishes a card describing its capabilities and accepts tasks from peer agents. In agent-to-tool protocols (MCP ), an agent connects to servers exposing tools and invokes them. In both, real deployments chain: an orchestrator delegates to a specialist, the specialist delegates to a tool, the tool calls a service. Work is routed through delegation, and the delegating party is frequently not the party the end user engaged.

When an action is later disputed — a payment made, a message sent, a record modified, a measurement commissioned — the operative questions are: under whose authority was this action taken, what exactly was authorized, what exactly was done, and can any of that be checked by someone who trusts none of the parties. Today the answers live in the logs of the parties to the dispute, which is to say they are not answers; they are claims. The sibling document treats the tamper-evidence of such logs. This document treats the prior question: what evidence should exist, at each hop, for a delegation chain to be checkable at all.

The scope is deliberately narrow. This document does not define a delegation protocol, a capability system, or an authorization framework. It defines the evidence requirements: which signed artifacts must exist at each hop, what each must reference, and what a verifier can conclude from them. Existing authorization machinery (tokens, capabilities) answers "may this action proceed". Delegation evidence answers the later question: "it proceeded — under whose grant, and is that answer checkable."

section.title: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: This document is Informational and contains no normative requirements.

dd.t: The agent (or its operator) granting authority to act.
The agent receiving the grant and performing actions under it.
A signed statement by the delegator authorizing a scoped class of actions by a named delegate, for a stated period or task. The grant is the unit of authority.
A signed statement by the delegate recording one action taken under a grant, referencing the grant by digest.

A signed statement, issued by the party receiving a call, acknowledging that a specified request was received and a specified response returned, bound to the request by digest. Receipts make a call checkable without trusting either party's logs.
A sequence in which a delegate under one grant acts as delegator for a further grant (sub-delegation), where the further grant is within the scope of the one under which the delegator itself acts.
An independent, append-only, publicly auditable log in which digests of grants, action records, or receipts are included, per , Section 4.3.

section.title: The Delegation Problem
section.t: Consider the minimal interesting case: agent A engages agent B to perform a task; B delegates part of it to agent C; C invokes tool T. The action that matters — say, a payment — is performed by T under a request from C, which C made under a grant from B, which B made under an engagement from A. Four properties of this shape drive the evidence requirements:

ul.li: Authority and action are separated in space and time. The grant exists before the action, is issued by a different party, and may cover many actions. Evidence must bind each action to the specific grant under which it was taken, not merely to the delegating party generally.

Each hop has an incentive asymmetry. When things go well, all parties claim credit; when they go badly, each party's incentive is to widen its own grant's scope retrospectively ("C was authorized to do that") or to narrow it ("C exceeded its authority"). Only a grant signed before the action, with its scope fixed and witnessed, resists both directions of revision.

The verifier trusts no one in the chain. The dispute may be precisely between the parties whose logs would otherwise answer the question. Evidence that resolves it must be checkable against keys and witnesses that are independent of every party to the dispute.

Chains fail at the joints. In practice the artifacts at each hop (a token presented, a call logged) exist; what is missing is the binding between them: the action record that names its grant by digest, the receipt that names its request by digest. The unbound middle — an action that references no grant, a grant under which no actions are recorded — is where disputes go to be unresolvable.

section.t: The sub-delegation case sharpens the third property. If B's grant to C purports to exceed B's own authority under A's engagement, the chain is only as strong as the scope check at that joint. Section 4.4 treats scope containment as a first-class verification step rather than an assumption.

section.title: Evidence Requirements
section.t: The requirements are stated as what must exist, not how it is encoded. COSE_Sign1 registered per is one adequate carrier; JWS over JSON is another. Where digests identify artifacts, the framing considerations of apply.

section.title: The Grant
section.t: A grant MUST-equivalent (this document is informational; the word marks a requirement for the evidence property, not a protocol mandate) carry:

G1. The delegator's identity, bound to a verification key whose resolution does not depend on the delegator's say-so (a DID, a SCITT-registered identity, a key published at a well-known location with its own witnessed history).
G2. The delegate's identity, with the same property.

G3. A scope: the class of actions authorized, stated tightly enough that an action can later be classified as in-scope or out-of-scope by inspection. "Handle the task" is not a scope; "invoke tool T with parameter class P, at most N times, spending at most X" is.
G4. A validity window or a task binding. Open-ended grants make temporal reasoning impossible: an action under an expired grant must be visibly under an expired grant.
G5. A statement of sub-delegation permission: may the delegate re-grant, and if so under what containment rule (strict narrowing is the only rule that composes safely).

G6. The delegator's signature over the above, and — for the grant to resist retrospective revision — witnessed inclusion of the grant's digest in an independent log before the actions under it commence, or at minimum before any dispute.
G6 is the requirement that is cheapest to meet before it is needed and impossible to meet after: a grant first published during a dispute is a claim about the past, not a record of it.

section.title: The Action Record
section.t: Each action taken under a grant produces an action record by the delegate carrying:
A1. The delegate's identity and signature.
A2. The digest of the grant under which the action is taken. This is the binding the problem of Section 3 turns on: not a reference to the delegator, but to the specific signed grant.
A3. A description of the action sufficient for scope classification: the tool invoked, the parameter class, the amount, the counterparty.
A4. A timestamp and, where the delegate keeps a hash-chained log per , the entry's position in that chain, so the action record cannot later be detached from its context without detection.
A5. Where a receipt (Section 4.3) is obtained from the receiving party, the receipt's digest.

The action record answers "what was done, under which grant". It does not answer "was the action correct" — that is measurement territory, out of scope here per 's separation of measurement from judgement.

section.title: The Receipt
section.t: A receipt is issued by the receiving party of a call (the agent accepting a task, the tool server accepting an invocation) and carries:
R1. The digest of the request as received — the exact octets, retained verbatim, since re-serialization changes digests in ways measured in .
R2. The digest of the response returned, or a statement that the request was refused.
R3. The receiving party's identity and signature, with key resolution independent of the issuer.
R4. Optionally, witnessed inclusion of the receipt digest, for calls whose later existence may be contested.

The receipt's function is to change what is being trusted. Without it, the caller's record of the call is the caller's claim, and the receiver's record is the receiver's claim, and a dispute is two claims. With it, both parties hold the same signed artifact and the verifier checks arithmetic. A signature is an integrity claim, not a truth claim: the receipt says these bytes were received and these bytes returned; it says nothing about whether the response was adequate. A content address is not authorization: the request digest proves identity of bytes, while whether the caller was authorized to make the request is established by the grant chain, not by the receipt.

section.title: Chain Composition
section.t: For a delegation chain of depth k, verification composes:

ol.li: Each action record references its grant by digest (A2); the referenced grant is fetched and its signature verified (G6).
The action is classified against the grant's scope (G3). The classification is a judgement a verifier makes by inspection; the evidence makes the judgement checkable, not automatic.

Where the grant's delegator was itself a delegate, the containing grant is fetched and the containment check applied: the sub-grant's scope must be within the containing scope. Strict narrowing (G5) is what makes this check decidable.
Each hop's witnessed digests are checked against the witness log's published history, establishing that the grants and receipts existed when claimed.

The verifier reports which links hold and which are absent. An action whose grant is missing, expired, out-of-scope, or unwitnessed is reported as such; the vocabulary of (through UNCHECKABLE for a broken chain) applies to each artifact.

section.t: The composition has one deliberately unfriendly property: it surfaces gaps rather than interpolating across them. A chain with an unwitnessed middle hop is not "mostly verified"; the middle hop is reported unwitnessed. Interpolation is how unresolvable disputes are manufactured.

section.title: Verification Without Trusted Central Parties
section.t: The verifier's complete trust set, with the requirements of Section 4 met:

ul.li: Signature verification against keys resolved from DIDs, well-known endpoints, or a transparency service's identity registry — none of which are parties to the dispute.
The append-only property of the witness log, which is publicly auditable and is the same trust a transparency log asks of the Internet .
Where anchors are used, the replication of the anchoring chain .

section.t: Nothing in the set is operated by any party to the delegation chain, and no account with anyone is required. The cost of this independence is paid at issuance time: keys must be published before they are needed, grants witnessed before actions, receipts collected at call time. The evidence cannot be back-constructed, which is precisely its value.

The pattern is deliberately indifferent to the transport. Whether the call travelled over an A2A task, an MCP tool invocation, or an ad-hoc HTTP request changes the encoding of the artifacts and none of the requirements. Delegation evidence is a property of the artifacts, not of the protocol that carried the call.

section.title: What Verification Does Not Establish
section.t: A verified delegation chain establishes: these grants existed at these times, signed by these keys; these actions reference those grants; these actions classify in or out of those scopes; these receipts bind these requests and responses. It does not establish:

ul.li: That the delegator's operator authorized the delegator. The chain of authority from an agent's key to a legal person is a separate evidentiary problem (key ceremony, organizational attestation) that this document does not address.
That the action was wise, lawful, or adequate. Verification binds action to authority; it does not grade either.

That no other actions occurred. Action records are positive evidence. The completeness question — was everything the delegate did recorded — is the log-integrity question of applied to the delegate, and composes with this document but is not solved by it.
That the identities are whom the end user believed them to be. Key-to-name binding is a discovery and naming problem; the evidence here binds keys to keys.

section.t: These exclusions are stated because the natural marketing summary of delegation evidence — "provably accountable agents" — claims all four. The artifacts claim none of them, and an honest deployment says so.

section.title: Relationship to Existing Work
section.t: The components exist and are not claimed here as new. Capability systems and macaroons-style attenuated tokens implement strict narrowing as an authorization mechanism; this document requires the same containment as an evidence property. The SCITT architecture and its reference APIs carry registration and receipts for signed statements; grants, action records, and receipts as defined here are signed statements. The CCF receipt profile is one receipt format with the required binding properties. A transparency log and Sigstore supply the witness pattern and a running public witness. The A2A protocol's agent card is a discovery surface to which delegation-evidence capabilities can be advertised; the MCP tool model is the other end of the same hop. The framing hazards for digest-identified CBOR artifacts are measured in ; the log-integrity substrate is ; the state vocabulary for reporting verification outcomes is .

What this document adds is the requirement set itself: the list of artifacts, the bindings between them, and the explicit statement of what verifying them does not establish. Existing protocol work has focused on making delegation work; this document is about making it checkable afterwards, which is a different design pressure and pulls artifacts into existence that working systems do not otherwise produce — most importantly, the pre-action witnessed grant (G6) and the request-bound receipt (Section 4.3).

section.title: Honesty and Scope
section.t: This section states what this document does not claim.

ul.li: This document does not define a delegation protocol, an authorization framework, or a capability system. It defines evidence requirements that such systems can meet.
This document does not claim that delegation evidence makes agents accountable. It makes specific claims checkable; accountability is a social property that evidence serves but does not constitute.
This document does not claim adoption by A2A, MCP, or any other protocol effort, and no statement here should be read as implying such adoption.
This document does not propose changes to any existing protocol. It composes existing machinery.
This document does not address key-to-legal-person binding, grant revocation semantics, or cross-jurisdictional evidential weight. All three matter and none are solved here.

The author operates a measurement service that issues signed receipts of the kind Section 4.3 describes, under a published A2A extension proposal. No conclusion about that service's quality follows from anything written here, and the extension proposal's existence does not imply its adoption by anyone.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: Grant theft and replay. A witnessed, signed grant is a bearer instrument for its scope unless the delegate identity (G2) is bound and checked at action time. Action records that name their grant (A2) allow a verifier to detect a delegate acting under a grant issued to another delegate; transport-level enforcement of the same check is a protocol decision outside this document.

Scope drafting. The containment check of Section 4.4 is only as strong as the scopes are legible. A scope written in natural language classifies by argument; a scope written in structured parameter classes classifies by inspection. Evidence requirements cannot force good drafting, but they can make bad drafting visible, since the classification step is reported.

Timing. Pre-action witnessing (G6) is the load-bearing timing requirement. A grant witnessed after the actions under it commenced is evidence of publication, not of prior existence, and honest reporting distinguishes the two — as do the pending and confirmed anchoring states of .

Framing hazards. Digest-identified artifacts over re-serializable encodings are subject to the class measured in ; received octets must be retained verbatim (R1) or a canonical encoding defined and enforced.
Witness trust. As in , Section 9: the witness's append-only property is the trust assumption, it is publicly auditable, and a verifier who does not audit it is trusting rather than verifying.
